The first loaves were bricks, dense and pale, and the sourdough starter died twice before I figured out the feeding schedule. My grandmother laughed and told me stories about her own early failures, the collapsed cakes and burnt pies of her youth, and insisted that patience mattered more than precision. By November I was waking before dawn to knead dough in the quiet dark, listening to the radio while the dough rose slowly beside the radiator. Friends started dropping by on Saturday mornings to taste the experiments, offering blunt opinions about crust and crumb, salt levels and browning. I adjusted hydration, tried longer ferments, switched to a heavier baking stone, and kept a notebook full of timings and temperatures. The village fair announced a baking contest for December, and on a whim I entered a walnut and honey loaf I had only made twice before. The morning of the contest the kitchen was freezing, the dough rose sluggishly, and I nearly gave up and stayed home. Instead I wrapped the loaf carefully, carried it across the snow to the fair hall, and set it among dozens of polished entries from far more experienced bakers. When the judges finished their slow round of tasting and whispering, they announced the winners, and to my complete astonishment the whole risky venture turned out perfectly.
